headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: AMGN, QCOM, EXPE, CRWV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Stryker – The medical equipment maker dropped more than 7% after management said Stryker's peripheral vascular business is suffering from supply constraints that are expected to act as a headwind through the third quarter and into the fourth quarter of the year. Amgen – The biotech stock slid almost 10%. Rival Novartis' cholesterol drug pelacarsen fell short in a closely watched study. In turn, this lowered traders' expectations for Amgen's olpasiran ahead of late-stage data due in 2027 or early 2028. BMO Capital Markets also cut its rating on Amgen to market perform, but kept its price target at $450, suggesting upside of just 3%. Qualcomm – The chipmaker jumped 4%. Qualcomm entered a data center infrastructure partnership with Amazon Web Services. As part of the deal, Qualcomm said it issued Amazon warrants to buy 25 million shares for $4 billion. Artificial intelligence infrastructure – Shares of companies linked to the AI buildout surged after OpenAI released its GPT-6 Astra large language model late last week. CoreWeave climbed almost 15%, while photonics stocks Lumentum and Coherent gained 12% and 9%, respectively. Fiber optic provider Corning and AI cloud play Nebius were each up 10%. Travel stocks — Shares of travel and lodging companies slid as gasoline futures rose. Expedia Group and Booking Holdings fell 6% and 5%, respectively. Tripadvisor and Airbnb dropped about 3%. Gasoline futures for October delivery were last up about 2%. Roivant Sciences — Shares rallied about 20% after the pharmaceutical company said Phase 2 trial results for subsidiary Pulmovant's mosliciguat demonstrated "a clinically meaningful and statistically significant placebo-adjusted reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance" in patients with pulmonary hypertension with interstitial lung disease. Lockheed Martin — The defense contractor added about 3% after UBS upgraded Lockheed to buy from neutral, citing underappreciated earnings growth potential . Novartis — The Swiss drugmaker tumbled 13% after Phase 3 results showed its del-desiran drug led to no significant improvement in patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1. This trial result was the third drug-trial disappointment for the company in a week. Peloton Interactive — Shares slid more than 5% after Morgan Stanley downgraded its investment recommendation to underweight from equal weight. "PTON is facing structural headwinds in fitness," the investment bank said. Boston Scientific — The medical device maker dropped 5% after BSX said a recent cyberattack likely hurt sales and profit targets for 2026 . Bloom Energy – The fuel-cell manufacturer jumped 10% in advance of joining the S & P 500 on Sept. 21. Bloom has been a major beneficiary of the AI data center buildout. Its shares are almost a triple this year, soaring about 190%. Quantum computing stocks – The quantum computing sector rallied after the U.S. agreed to take minority equity stakes in several companies as part of a $300 million CHIPS Act deal. The investments are in D-Wave Quantum , Rigetti Computing and Quantinuum . D-Wave gained more than 7%, Rigetti rose 4% and Quantinuum added 3%. —CNBC's Christina Cheddar Berk, Nick Wells and Darla Mercado contributed to this report.

In this article 1810-HK AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:36 04:36 New foldable competitors to iPhone: Here's what to know Squawk Box Huawei and Xiaomi this week rolled out their latest foldable phones as the Chinese tech giants look to steal a lead on rival Apple , which is rumored to launch its first foldable iPhone on Wednesday. Xiaomi , the world's third-largest smartphone player, launched the Xiaomi 18 Fold on Monday, a passport-sized device similar to Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold8, which was released earlier this year . Huawei on Monday unveiled the Mate XT2, the third generation of its trifold smartphone , which it pioneered. Those launches are no coincidence. Apple is holding an event on Wednesday , where it is rumored to be unveiling the first foldable iPhone, a major new product under new CEO John Ternus . "There is significant pent-up demand for a foldable iPhone within the Apple community," Neil Shah, partner at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC on Tuesday. "Many have refrained from switching to Samsung. Some have switched, but they might come back if there is an amazing foldable iPhone." Apple could ship 6 million foldable iPhones this year, giving it a 25% share of the global market, according to Counterpoint Research. This share could grow to 40% in 2027, Counterpoint said. Foldable smartphones continue to see strong growth, even though they are some of the most expensive handsets on the market. "We will see lots of upgrades from the existing install base in China happening toward the foldable iPhone," Shah said. "This is not an innocent decision by these vendors," Francisco Jeronimo, a vice president at IDC covering mobile devices, told CNBC. "They knew Apple was coming up with a foldable, so they're trying to get ahead and, more importantly, trying to make sure that when the Apple products hit the stores, their product is there so consumers can compare." Huawei and Xiaomi chips Huawei and Xiaomi this week touted their own self-designed chips in their foldables. Xiaomi said the Xiaomi 18 Fold is powered by the XRing O3, its latest smartphone processor, manufactured on an advanced process. headlines.title: Qualcomm issues Amazon warrants to acquire $4 billion worth of chipmaker's stock as part of AI infrastructure deal
headlines.summary: Qualcomm is trying to move into the data center business, where Nvidia has been the dominant player in the AI boom.
headlines.article_text: Qualcomm issues Amazon warrants to acquire 25 million shares Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Qualcomm said it's working with Amazon across "multiple generations of customized silicon" to help build out AWS' AI infrastructure. The chipmaker is trying to move into the data center business, where Nvidia has been the dominant player in the AI boom. Qualcomm issued Amazon warrants to acquire 25 million shares. In this article QCOM AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:08 04:08 Qualcomm to build chips for Amazon Squawk on the Street Qualcomm shares rose 4% on Tuesday after the company announced a data center infrastructure partnership with Amazon Web Services, a major win as the chipmaker tries to take on Nvidia in the artificial intelligence market. As part of the agreement, Qualcomm said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it issued Amazon warrants to acquire 25 million shares in the company at $161.26 apiece for a total investment of $4 billion. According to a press release about the technology pact, Qualcomm is working with Amazon "across multiple generations of customized silicon" to help build out AWS' AI infrastructure, specifically focused on inference. "As AI workloads grow exponentially — driving unprecedented demand for compute, storage, networking and memory bandwidth, and energy-efficient infrastructure — the collaboration brings together Amazon's comprehensive, secure, and price-performant AI infrastructure with Qualcomm Technologies' leadership in power-efficient processing, silicon design and system-level integration," the statement said. Qualcomm is known for making processors that power smartphones and other mobile devices. But the company made a big splash in June, when it revealed a central processing unit for data centers called Dragonfly C1000, and said that Meta would use it when it starts production in 2028. The chipmaker said the new CPU was built for agentic AI and focuses on offering computing performance without using too much power. Qualcomm said at the time that it's targeting $15 billion in data center sales in fiscal 2029, and pointed to a road map for going after the market with several different products, including an AI chip and a product that will tie multiple chips together. Read more CNBC tech news 'Model fatigue' sets in as AI labs race to roll out new versions at frenetic pace Meet the CISO: A new front-line star in the AI cybersecurity war Mistral bags $24 billion valuation as Samsung leads funding for Europe's AI champion TSMC, Samsung commit to ASML's newest chipmaking tools as AI drives demand In teaming up with AWS, Qualcomm is getting a show of confidence from another hyperscaler. Like Meta, Amazon's annual capital expenditures on AI infrastructure are reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars. Qualcomm's warrant to Amazon expires on Sept. 3, 2036. The company said the shares vest in tranches tied to the "execution of certain commercial arrangements," as well as the purchase of up to $60 billion worth of Qualcomm's server chips and other technology. Nvidia has emerged as the world's most valuable company by dominating the market for graphics processing units, or GPUs, which are needed for building sophisticated AI models and running the heftiest workloads. But more chipmakers are getting involved in the AI boom now that the CPU is proving key for AI. While GPUs are ideal for training and running AI models because they have thousands of tiny cores narrowly focused on performing many operations simultaneously, CPUs have a smaller number of powerful cores running sequential general purpose tasks. Bank of America predicts the CPU market could more than double, from $27 billion in 2025 to $60 billion by 2030. Intel and Advanced Micro Devices are both seeing surging demand for their data center CPUs, and Nvidia in March offered new details about its agentic-optimized CPUs. Dion Harris, Nvidia's head of AI infrastructure, told CNBC at the time that, "CPUs are becoming the bottleneck in terms of growing out this AI and agentic workflow." — CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report. headlines.article_text: UK announces Israeli settlement sanctions despite U.S. economic warnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The U.K. has announced a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. It will also ban arms exports to the settlements. U.S. officials and lawmakers warned British companies could face business restrictions in some states. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arriving for a Cabinet meeting in Downing Street, London. Picture date: Tuesday September 8, 2026. Stefan Rousseau | Pa Images | Getty Images The U.K. government is pushing ahead with planned sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, despite U.S. officials and lawmakers warning of economic consequences for doing so. Speaking in the country's parliament on Tuesday, U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain would ban imports from Israeli settlements built on land that is internationally recognized as Palestinian territory. The measures are expected to take six to nine months to come into force, he added. "Today I announce that the official view of the British government is that the occupation [of the West Bank] is unlawful," Miliband told British lawmakers. "The government believes the unlawfulness of the occupation should be reflected in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories." Miliband said the British government agreed that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, "perpetrated by settler terrorists." NORTHERN WEST BANK, WEST BANK - SEPTEMBER 8: An Israeli flag is hang on a sign showing the way to the Palestinian city of Nablus on September 8, 2026 in Northern West Bank, West Bank. The UK government implements a comprehensive trade ban and targeted sanctions on goods and services from the illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. (Photo by Amir Levy/Getty Images) Amir Levy | Getty Images News | Getty Images "All too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this, and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the displacement of Palestinians," he said. "It should be the prelude to justice." Shortly after the sanctions were announced, the Israeli government announced it would close the British consulate in Jerusalem. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the British government was "systematically working against the state of Israel." Twelve U.K. politicians were also banned from entering Israel. Alongside the roll-out of a "comprehensive sanctions regime," Miliband said the British government would take action against specific companies and individuals that provide services such as construction, infrastructure, or financing for real estate expansion by settlers. The U.K. will also ban advertisements related to the settlements. "To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: you will face the full force of U.K. sanctions," he said, but he stressed that the U.K. would continue to trade with Israel, "precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel." However, Miliband said the U.K. would also extend a ban on arms exports to include refusing all license applications for arms and other goods and services "that materially contribute to the occupation." He called this an effective "double lock against arms sales" after the U.K. suspended over 30 arms licenses used by the Israel Defense Forces in Gaza. "This means the ban on such exports will now remain in place as long as the occupation exists," he told lawmakers. Last week, Miliband told lawmakers that Israel's recent issuance of tenders for the E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank was "the crossing of a red line." "Israeli settlements are illegal under international law," he said at the time. "This Government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution — we will act. I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "Obviously we're not going to do what the UK did." "We think it has implications as well on our ability to make progress with regards to Gaza, on the 20-point plan and the Board of Peace that we're very committed to," he added. In this article NVS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT FILE PHOTO: The logo of Swiss drugmaker Novartis is seen at the company's new cell and gene therapy factory in Stein, Switzerland, November 28, 2019. Arnd Wiegmann | Reuters Novartis shares tanked on Tuesday after the pharmaceutical giant said its del-desiran drug for muscle-wasting disorder failed in a late-stage trial. The company's stock was down almost 10.5% in late afternoon trade, as investors reacted to what was its third drug trial setback in a week. It put the shares on track for their worst trading day since March 2020. Novartis stock The del-desiran result comes just days after Novartis said its pelacarsen drug failed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in a late-stage trial, and a week after announcing it had paused eight clinical trials of an experimental cell therapy, rap-cel, after three patients died. Muscle-wasting disorder trial Novartis said its global phase III HARBOR study, which had been testing del-desiran in patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1, failed to show that the drug significantly improved patients' ability to open their hands faster than a placebo. "Novartis is evaluating the full HARBOR dataset and will engage with health authorities to determine the most appropriate development path for del-desiran," the company said in a news release. "Developing therapies for a complex disease like [myotonic dystrophy type 1] remains challenging, and setbacks are part of scientific progress," Shreeram Aradhye, president of development and chief medical officer at Novartis, said in a statement Tuesday.
